guidance: Read the figure and its unit off the water report before converting: a US report is usually mg/L as calcium carbonate or grains per US gallon, a German one in degrees dH and a French one in degrees fH. The USGS class is a general guideline for a supply, so size a softener from its own capacity rating and the report rather than from the class alone.
method: Water hardness counts the divalent calcium and magnesium in a sample as an equivalent mass of calcium carbonate, so every scale here is the same quantity in a different unit. The tool works in milligrams per litre as CaCO3. One millimole per litre of CaCO3 is 100.0869 mg/L, the molar mass of calcium carbonate. One German degree (dH, dGH) is 10 mg of calcium oxide per litre, which is 10/56.0774 mmol/L, or 17.8479922 mg/L as CaCO3. One English or Clark degree is one grain of calcium carbonate per imperial gallon and one grain per US gallon (gpg) is one grain per US gallon; with the international grain of exactly 64.79891 mg, the imperial gallon of 4.54609 L and the US gallon of 3.785411784 L those are 14.2537675 and 17.1180610 mg/L, so the same water reads about 1.2 times higher in gpg than in Clark degrees. One French degree is 10 mg/L by definition. Each converted value is rounded to six significant figures and displayed to four, so a catalog case can state the exact number the page shows. Entries are accepted from 0 to 100,000 mg/L as CaCO3, which spans distilled water to the hardest brines; a negative entry or a figure above that ceiling is refused rather than clipped. The class follows the USGS general guidelines in mg/L as CaCO3: up to 60 soft, 61 to 120 moderately hard, 121 to 180 hard and above 180 very hard. Those bands describe a water supply rather than a treatment decision: they say nothing about a softener capacity, the resin or a local utility scale, so a report in another unit should be converted before it is compared with them. The tool does not split carbonate from non-carbonate hardness, does not use alkalinity, pH or temperature, measures nothing itself, and runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: USGS Water Science School, Hardness of Water: general guidelines classify water as soft at 0 to 60 mg/L as calcium carbonate, moderately hard at 61 to 120, hard at 121 to 180 and very hard above 180.

Wikipedia, Hard water: hardness is reported as calcium carbonate equivalents, with the conversion table between mmol/L, mg/L, German degrees, grains per US gallon, English (Clark) degrees and French degrees used to cross-check this tool's factors.
